text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • Culturally safe care: address him as Mr. Kahanamoku, as he asked; take time; explain each test and medicine plainly; involve his ʻohana as he chooses while he makes the decisions
  • Heart failure cardiology consultation on the day of the two-week visit, with an echocardiogram, to confirm the diagnosis and its cause and to plan guideline-directed medical therapy, ischemic evaluation and device decisions
  • Furosemide 40 mg every morning for congestion, with a daily weight and a written plan; metabolic panel and magnesium in one to two weeks; lower the dose when he is dry
  • Baseline tests: ECG, chest X-ray, NT-proBNP, metabolic panel and magnesium, blood count, iron studies, TSH, hemoglobin A1c, lipids and ALT; echocardiogram at the two-week visit
  • Atorvastatin raised from 40 to 80 mg for LDL 92 mg/dL; lipid panel in four to twelve weeks; goal below 70 mg/dL
  • Sodium: less salted and dried fish, shoyu and salty party food, using the foods he already eats; no routine fluid restriction; daily weights
  • Vaccinations: pneumococcal, influenza, COVID-19 and RSV as due, because heart disease raises the risk of severe respiratory infection
  • Native Hawaiian healing alongside clinic care, if he wishes: lomilomi through Ke Ola Mamo, a Native Hawaiian Health Care System; he will tell the clinic before using any plant medicine so that interactions can be checked; the clinic asks nothing further about his practices
  • Guideline-directed medical therapy: stop lisinopril and start sacubitril-valsartan 24/26 mg twice daily 36 hours after the last dose; change metoprolol tartrate to carvedilol 3.125 mg twice daily; empagliflozin 10 mg daily; add spironolactone when potassium and kidney function allow; raise one medicine every two weeks toward target doses, with a metabolic panel one to two weeks after each change
  • Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose 750 mg at the two-week visit and again two weeks later, for iron deficiency in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction; iron studies again at about six months
  • Invasive coronary angiography within two weeks to define the coronary disease and whether revascularization could help
  • Defibrillator decision: repeat echocardiogram after at least 90 days of optimized therapy; a primary-prevention ICD if the ejection fraction stays at 35% or below with NYHA class II to III
  • Sick-day rules: on days of vomiting, diarrhea or not drinking, hold empagliflozin, furosemide, spironolactone and sacubitril-valsartan, keep carvedilol if blood pressure allows, drink small amounts often, and restart when eating and drinking normally for a day; a written card
  • Cardiac rehabilitation for heart failure, 36 sessions, adapted to an ocean athlete: pool swimming in the program, then calm water inside the reef with a companion and near a lifeguard, no breath-hold diving, no big surf until cleared, water through the morning, and out of the water at once for chest pain, lightheadedness or unusual breathlessness
  • Laboratory tests drawn at the clinic on the day of each medicine change or by the clinic's nurse at home, with nurse calls to titrate doses between visits

resource.title: Duke Kahanamoku synthetic care plan
resource.description: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction from ischemic cardiomyopathy in a 66-year-old Native Hawaiian man, sheriff of Honolulu and a lifelong Olympic swimmer and surfer, five years after a heart attack. The episode covers breathlessness, ankle swelling and tiredness diagnosed by NT-proBNP and echocardiography (ejection fraction 30%); invasive coronary angiography for the ischemic cause; the four pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy under the 1953 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline and the 1955 ACC decision pathway: changing lisinopril to sacubitril-valsartan with a 36-hour washout, changing metoprolol tartrate to carvedilol, empagliflozin and spironolactone, titrated every two weeks with potassium, magnesium and kidney checks; a loop diuretic adjusted to euvolemia; intravenous iron for iron deficiency; sick-day rules when vomiting and diarrhea raise potassium and creatinine; a missed laboratory check recorded honestly; the decision against a primary-prevention defibrillator when the ejection fraction rose from 30% to 38% after more than 90 days of therapy; sodium guidance without routine fluid restriction; cardiac rehabilitation adapted to an ocean athlete, with swimming and surfing safety; vaccinations; and culturally safe care for a Native Hawaiian patient, with his ʻohana involved as he chooses, his own healing practices respected, and attention to the higher and earlier burden of heart failure hospitalization among Native Hawaiians.
